section.title: The Weeping Prophet
section.sectionRationale: This is the heart of Jeremiah's grief, the passage that has earned him the name the weeping prophet. Judah's wound proves incurable, false healers keep crying peace where there is no peace, and in the middle of the wreckage stands the one boast still open to sinners, to know the LORD who delights in loving devotion, justice, and righteousness.
section.thesis: Judah refuses to turn back despite warning after warning, and the coming judgment breaks even the prophet who announces it, yet true wisdom is not found in cleverness, strength, or wealth but only in knowing the LORD, whose own heart is set on steadfast love, justice, and righteousness.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Judah's stubborn refusal to repent and the false healers who cry peace where there is none; the prophet's own grief that there is no balm for so great a wound; his wish to weep without ceasing and God's charge of pervasive deceit; a summons to lament for the land God will make desolate; and the true boast, not in wisdom, strength, or wealth, but in knowing the LORD.

units.label: No one repents
units.note: false healers cry peace where there is none

verses.text:
So you are to tell them this is what the LORD says: 
“Do men fall and not get up again? Does one turn away and not return?
Why then have these people turned away? Why does Jerusalem always turn away? They cling to deceit; they refuse to return.
I have listened and heard; they do not speak what is right. No one repents of his wickedness, asking, ‘What have I done?’ Everyone has pursued his own course like a horse charging into battle.
Even the stork in the sky knows her appointed seasons. The turtledove, the swift, and the thrush keep their time of migration, but My people do not know the requirements of the LORD.
How can you say, ‘We are wise, and the Law of the LORD is with us,’ when in fact the lying pen of the scribes has produced a deception?
The wise will be put to shame; they will be dismayed and trapped. Since they have rejected the word of the LORD, what wisdom do they really have?
Therefore I will give their wives to other men and their fields to new owners. For from the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit.
They dress the wound of the daughter of My people with very little care, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace at all.
I will take away their harvest, declares the LORD. There will be no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the tree, and even the leaf will wither. Whatever I have given them will be lost to them.”

units.label: Is there no balm in Gilead?

verses.text: Why are we just sitting here? Gather together, let us flee to the fortified cities and perish there, for the LORD our God has doomed us. He has given us poisoned water to drink, because we have sinned against the LORD.
We hoped for peace, but no good has come, for a time of healing, but there was only terror.

The snorting of enemy horses is heard from Dan. At the sound of the neighing of mighty steeds, the whole land quakes. They come to devour the land and everything in it, the city and all who dwell in it.

“For behold, I will send snakes among you, vipers that cannot be charmed, 
and they will bite you,” declares the LORD.
My sorrow is beyond healing; my heart is faint within me.

Listen to the cry of the daughter of my people from a land far away: 
“Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?” 
“Why have they provoked Me to anger with their carved images, 
with their worthless foreign idols?”
“The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.”
For the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am crushed. I mourn; horror has gripped me.
Is there no {{tsori|balm}} in Gilead? Is no physician there? Why then has the health of the daughter of my people not been restored?

units.label: Oh, that my head were a spring of water
units.note: a wish to weep without ceasing

verses.text: Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears! I would {{bakah|weep}} day and night over the slain daughter of my people.
If only I had a traveler’s lodge in the wilderness, I would abandon my people and depart from them, for they are all adulterers, a crowd of faithless people.
“They bend their tongues like bows; lies prevail over truth in the land. For they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not take Me into account,” declares the LORD.
“Let everyone guard against his neighbor; do not trust any brother, for every brother deals craftily, and every friend spreads slander.
Each one betrays his friend; no one tells the truth. They have taught their tongues to lie; they wear themselves out committing iniquity.
You dwell in the midst of deception; in their deceit they refuse to know Me,” declares the LORD.

Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says: 
“Behold, I will refine them and test them, for what else can I do 
because of the daughter of My people?
Their tongues are deadly arrows; they speak deception. With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him.
Should I not punish them for these things? declares the LORD. Should I not avenge Myself on such a nation as this?”

units.label: A lament for the land
units.note: wailing women summoned, corpses like dung

verses.text: I will take up a weeping and wailing for the mountains, a dirge over the wilderness pasture, for they have been scorched so no one passes through, and the lowing of cattle is not heard. Both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled; they have gone away.
“And I will make Jerusalem a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals; and I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.”
Who is the man wise enough to understand this? To whom has the mouth of the LORD spoken, that he may explain it? Why is the land destroyed and scorched like a desert, so no one can pass through it?
And the LORD answered, “It is because they have forsaken My law, which I set before them; they have not walked in it or obeyed My voice.
Instead, they have followed the stubbornness of their hearts and gone after the Baals, as their fathers taught them.”
Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: “Behold, I will feed this people wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink.
I will scatter them among the nations that neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send a sword after them until I have finished them off.”

This is what the LORD of Hosts says: 
“Take note, and summon the wailing women; send for the most skillful among them.
Let them come quickly and take up a lament over us, that our eyes may overflow with tears, and our eyelids may gush with water.
For the sound of wailing is heard from Zion: ‘How devastated we are! How great is our shame! For we have abandoned the land because our dwellings have been torn down.’”
Now, O women, hear the word of the LORD. Open your ears to the word of His mouth. Teach your daughters to wail, and one another to lament.
For death has climbed in through our windows; it has entered our fortresses to cut off the children from the streets, the young men from the town squares.

Declare that this is what the LORD says: 
“The corpses of men will fall like dung upon the open field, like newly cut grain behind the reaper, with no one to gather it.”

units.label: Let him who boasts, boast in this
units.note: true wisdom is knowing the LORD

verses.text:
This is what the LORD says: 
“Let not the wise man {{halal|boast}} in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, 
nor the wealthy man in his riches.

But let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth, for I delight in these things,” declares the LORD.
“Behold, the days are coming,” declares the LORD, “when I will punish all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised:

Egypt, Judah, Edom, Ammon, Moab, and all the inhabitants of the desert who clip the hair of their temples. For all these nations are uncircumcised, and the whole house of Israel is {{arel|uncircumcised}} in heart.”

tsori.gloss: Balm, a soothing resin used medicinally and prized in trade, associated with Gilead. Jeremiah's question exposes that Judah's wound goes past any earthly remedy; only the LORD Himself can heal what sin has broken.

bakah.gloss: To weep, to cry out in grief. Jeremiah's wish for a fountain of tears earns him the title the weeping prophet; his tears are not a failure of faith but the shape lived faith takes when covenant love meets covenant unfaithfulness.

halal.gloss: To boast or to praise; the same root gives Israel its word for praise, hallelujah. Here God redirects all boasting away from wisdom, strength, and riches to the one ground of true praise, knowing Him.

arel.gloss: Uncircumcised, used literally of the flesh and, startlingly, of the heart. Judah kept the sign of the covenant in the flesh while its heart remained untouched by God, showing the sign was always meant to point to a transformed inner life.

basic.context: Jeremiah has just delivered his temple sermon; now he turns inward and lets the grief of coming judgment wash over his own heart. Judah refuses to repent though the whole created order, even migrating birds, keeps its appointed times better than God's people know His requirements. False prophets and priests dress the nation's wound with a shallow, Peace, peace, when there is no peace, and Jeremiah is undone with sorrow, wishing his eyes were a fountain of tears.
basic.hermeneutics: This is poetry of lament woven through prophetic oracle so tightly that at points it is genuinely hard to tell whether Jeremiah or the LORD is speaking, or both at once. That is not a flaw; it shows how fully the prophet's heart has been shaped by God's own grief over His people. The passage also contains one of Scripture's most quoted lines on true boasting, verses 23 and 24, which Paul later picks up almost word for word.
basic.originalLanguages: Jeremiah asks whether there is tsori, balm, in Gilead, a region famous for a soothing medicinal resin, exposing that Judah's wound has gone past any remedy trade could supply. He wishes he could bakah, weep, day and night, giving him his lasting name, the weeping prophet. God redirects all halal, boasting, away from wisdom, strength, and wealth to knowing Him alone, and calls Judah arel, uncircumcised, in heart, even though the flesh still bore the covenant sign.
basic.typology: Jeremiah's tears over an unrepentant Jerusalem anticipate Jesus weeping over the same city centuries later. The impossible wound with no balm anticipates the true balm and physician, Christ, who alone heals what sin has broken. And the call to boast only in knowing the LORD anticipates the gospel logic Paul later makes explicit, that all boasting is excluded except in Christ.
basic.christ: Jesus stands in the line of Jeremiah as the weeping prophet magnified: He weeps over Jerusalem's hardness of heart, Luke 19:41-44, in language that echoes a physician grieving over a patient he cannot heal, recalling Jeremiah's balm in Gilead. Paul takes up Jeremiah 9:23-24 almost word for word in 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17: let him who boasts, boast in the Lord, because in Christ alone believers have wisdom, righteousness, and redemption to boast in.
basic.god: God is grieved by His people's sin in a way that defies easy categories; His words and Jeremiah's tears blend until the reader can no longer separate them. Yet in the middle of announced judgment God names what He delights in: loving devotion, justice, and righteousness on the earth. Even the harshest oracle in this passage serves the character God wants known and praised.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 19:41-44 has Jesus weep over Jerusalem much as Jeremiah weeps here. 1 Corinthians 1:26-31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17 quote Jeremiah 9:23-24 directly. Deuteronomy 10:16 and Romans 2:28-29 speak of circumcision of the heart, the very thing Judah lacked. Matthew 9:12 pictures Jesus as the physician the sick actually need.
basic.oneStory: This is the anguish of a shepherd's heart over a people who will not turn, carried by a prophet whose tears mirror God's own. Jesus is the greater weeping prophet, who weeps over the same city and provides the balm sin cannot heal on its own, so that the one boast left to sinners, knowing the LORD, becomes, in Christ, boasting in the wisdom, righteousness, and redemption He alone supplies.

context.literary:
This unit is a tapestry of voices, and the seams are the point. In the space of a few lines the speaker changes from the LORD, to the frightened people, to the prophet, to the LORD again, and Jeremiah does not label the changes. Verse 19 of chapter 8 is the clearest case: the prophet reports a far off cry, 'Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?', and the LORD answers, 'Why have they provoked Me to anger with their carved images?', and then the people speak once more, 'The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, but we have not been saved.' Three voices share two verses.

The unit moves in six steps. Verses 4 to 13 are a set of accusing questions: does anyone fall and not get up, does the stork know her seasons, where is your wisdom? Verses 14 to 17 give the city's panic. Verses 18 to 22 are the first full lament, ending with three questions about balm, physician and healing. Chapter 9, verses 1 to 9, begins with the prophet's wish for tears and then the longing to flee, followed by a portrait of a society of liars. Verses 10 to 16 are a dirge over the empty countryside, a question about why the land is ruined, and the LORD's answer. Verses 17 to 22 summon professional mourners, and verses 23 to 26 close with a short, pointed instruction about boasting and a warning that circumcision is not enough.

The English chapter division hides a little of this. The Hebrew Bible begins its chapter 9 one verse later than English, so that the cry 'Oh, that my head were a spring of water' belongs to the end of the chapter of lament, not the start of a new section. The tears run straight on from the question about the balm.

Two passages are repeated from earlier in the book. Verses 10 to 12 of chapter 8 are almost word for word Jeremiah 6:13-15, and 9:9 repeats the refrain of 5:9 and 5:29. The unit is thus a gathering of themes, a last chorus before the book turns from sermon to the personal confessions of the prophet. It ends with a triple in 9:23 and a triple in 9:24, wise, strong, rich, answered by loving devotion, justice and righteousness.
context.historical:
The setting is the reign of Jehoiakim, when the nation had been hurt by the death of Josiah and was struggling between Egypt and the rising power of Babylon. The panic of 8:14, 'Gather together, let us flee to the fortified cities,' is the reflex of a country within sight of an enemy, and verse 16 locates the enemy: the snorting of horses is heard from Dan, the northern frontier town. Jeremiah 4:15 had already said 'a voice resounds from Dan.' The first alarm is at the far end of the land.

Gilead lay east of the Jordan, and it had long been known for its balm. Joseph's brothers saw a caravan coming from Gilead 'carrying spices, balm, and myrrh' on their way to Egypt, Genesis 37:25, and Jacob later told his sons to take 'a little balm' as a gift, Genesis 43:11. The question 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' was therefore a question about one of the best known cures of the world Jeremiah's hearers lived in. Jeremiah 46:11 uses the same image of Egypt, 'In vain you try many remedies.'

The scribes of verse 8 were the professional keepers of the Law. Shaphan the scribe read the Book of the Law to Josiah, 2 Kings 22:8-11, and Baruch the scribe wrote down Jeremiah's own words, Jeremiah 36:4. By the time of this sermon the written word of God carried great prestige, and people could point to it and say, 'The Law of the LORD is with us.' Jeremiah's charge is that having the book is not the same as having the word.

The birds of verse 7 point to the geography of the land. Israel sits on one of the great migration routes between Europe and Africa, and ordinary people watched the flocks come and go each year. The footnote in the BSB notes that the exact identification of some birds is uncertain, but the point is clear.

The wailing women of 9:17 belong to a real custom. Skilled mourners were hired for funerals, as Amos 5:16 shows, and Jeremiah himself lamented over Josiah, 2 Chronicles 35:25. The statement that death 'has climbed in through our windows' may echo a Canaanite picture of Death entering a house through the window, though the text does not claim it. The list in 9:26 names peoples whose customs included circumcision or clipping the temples, and Jeremiah 25:23 and 49:32 refer to the same desert peoples.
context.canonical:
The weeping of 9:1 belongs to a family of tears in the prophets. Jeremiah himself says, 'I will weep in secret because of your pride,' Jeremiah 13:17, and, 'My eyes overflow with tears,' Jeremiah 14:17. Isaiah cries, 'Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly,' Isaiah 22:4, and the psalmist writes, 'My eyes shed streams of tears because Your law is not obeyed,' Psalm 119:136. Lamentations carries on the voice, 'Streams of tears flow from my eyes over the destruction of the daughter of my people,' Lamentations 3:48. Behind the prophets stands God Himself, who before the flood 'was grieved in His heart,' Genesis 6:6, and who 'in all their distress was afflicted,' Isaiah 63:9.

The wound without remedy is also a recurring picture. 'Your injury is incurable,' Jeremiah 30:12, is answered, 'I will bring to it health and healing,' Jeremiah 33:6. Isaiah 1:6 describes a body with no soundness. The Gospels take up the figure of the doctor, 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick,' Mark 2:17.

The call to boast in the LORD is quoted twice by Paul. 'Let him who boasts boast in the Lord,' 1 Corinthians 1:31 and 2 Corinthians 10:17. In the first he places it at the end of an argument that God chose the foolish, weak and lowly so that 'no one may boast in His presence,' 1 Corinthians 1:27-29. He adds 'Christ Jesus, who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' verse 30. Galatians 6:14 puts it as personal confession: 'may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.'

Circumcision of the heart is another thread. Moses commands it, 'Circumcise your hearts, therefore, and stiffen your necks no more,' Deuteronomy 10:16, and promises that the LORD Himself will do it, Deuteronomy 30:6. Jeremiah 4:4 repeats the call. Paul says, 'circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit,' Romans 2:29, and Colossians 2:11 speaks of 'the circumcision performed by Christ.' Stephen's speech charges the leaders with 'uncircumcised hearts and ears,' Acts 7:51.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The purpose of this unit is to make the reader feel what the judgment costs. The earlier chapters of Jeremiah argued a case; here the lawyer weeps. The writer wants hearers to see that the announcement of exile was not delivered with relish. The prophet carries the sorrow of the people, and the LORD's own voice joins the lament. By giving these voices together the book teaches that true prophecy hurts the one who speaks it, which marks Jeremiah out from the prophets who say 'Peace, peace.'

The unit also gives the reason for the disaster in two forms. Verse 7 of chapter 8 says that creatures know their seasons while Israel does not know God's justice. Chapter 9 verses 12 to 14 give a direct answer to the question that every survivor would ask, 'Why is the land destroyed?' It is because 'they have forsaken My law, which I set before them; they have not walked in it or obeyed My voice.' The exiles were to read that answer as an explanation, not an accusation of God.

The closing verses are the writer's pointer to what would still stand. Wisdom, strength and wealth, the three things on which a nation relied in a crisis, are not worth boasting in. The one thing worth boasting in is knowing the LORD. The unit ends by telling the nation that its covenant sign, circumcision, did not distinguish it from Egypt or Edom if the heart stayed closed, and that the prophet's sorrow was aimed at a change of heart, not just a change of fortune.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of the chapter records speech and feeling: the people's panic, the prophet's grief, God's sentence. These are not commands. Jeremiah's wish in 9:2 to have a lodge in the wilderness and abandon his people is a cry of exhaustion, not a model for ministry, and it stands beside the wish of 9:1 to weep for them day and night. Scripture lets a prophet voice contradictory feelings in the same breath, and does not tell the reader to choose the first.

There are some instructions. The command in 9:17 to summon the wailing women and in 9:20 to 'teach your daughters to wail' is a call to the people to lament out loud in a time of disaster. It teaches that grief is a proper response to sin and judgment, and the New Testament echoes it in 'weep with those who weep,' Romans 12:15. It does not make professional mourning mandatory.

The clearest prescription is 9:23 and 24: let the one who boasts boast in knowing the LORD. This is a standing instruction, and Paul treats it that way. By contrast, the statements about nations in 9:25 and 26 describe a time when Judah's circumcision would not shield it, and should not be turned into a slur against anyone. They are a warning to those who rely on a sign. They apply to anyone who trusts membership in a church, a rite or a heritage in place of a heart that has been changed.

debates.question: Whose voice is weeping in 8:18 to 9:1?

views.label: Jeremiah's
views.case: The speaker uses the language of personal grief, 'my sorrow,' 'my heart,' 'my eyes,' and the prophet elsewhere describes weeping for the people, Jeremiah 13:17 and 14:17. On this view the verses show a prophet torn between his loyalty to God and his love for his people, and the book's Confessions are anticipated here.

views.label: The LORD's
views.case: Verse 19 has the LORD's own complaint, and the phrase 'daughter of My people' belongs to God in other passages. Isaiah 63:9 says God was afflicted in His people's affliction, and Hosea 11:8 shows His compassion stirred. On this reading the passage is a rare window into divine sorrow.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Many readers take the blending as deliberate. The prophet is so shaped by God's word that his grief and God's grief cannot be separated, which is also how a true prophet differs from one who speaks 'peace.' The ambiguity is the lesson.

debates.bearing: The third view fits the way the passage reads, and it matters for how believers speak of God. The Bible does not ask us to choose between a God who judges and a God who weeps. It shows them in the same breath, and later shows them in one person, Luke 19:41.

debates.question: What is the 'lying pen of the scribes' in 8:8?

views.label: Scribes who misused or altered the Law
views.case: The verse says the pen has 'produced a deception' even though the people claim to have the Law. Some take this to mean that scribes were writing and teaching distortions, perhaps in the form of interpretations or additions that excused the behaviour the Law condemned. Jesus' own charge that the traditions of men nullify the word of God, Mark 7:13, is a parallel.

views.label: A reference to the way the written Law was handled, not a charge of forgery
views.case: Others read the line as an attack on a confident use of the book, in which possession of the Law became a badge of wisdom. Whether the scribes distorted the text or only the way it was used, the result is the same: the word was in their hands and not in their hearts. This view fits the Josiah period, when the book had recently been found and read.

views.label: A specific reference to the scroll found in the temple
views.case: A smaller group connects the verse to the Book of the Law in 2 Kings 22 and suggests that Jeremiah is criticising how the reform used it. This is possible but not required by the text, which does not mention Josiah.

debates.bearing: All three agree that holding a holy text is no substitute for obeying it. The passage does not criticise the Law, which the next verse calls 'the word of the LORD,' but the confidence of those who thought owning it made them wise.

study.originalLanguages:
Jeremiah's favourite verb is shuv, to turn. In 8:4 and 5 it appears for both the falling away and the coming back: 'Does one turn away and not return?' The same verb does double duty on purpose, because in Jeremiah's preaching repentance is not a new act but the reversal of the old one. The word the BSB renders 'always' in the question about Jerusalem comes from a root meaning to be perpetual. The people are not stuck in a single lapse but in a standing habit of turning away.

In verse 7 the people 'do not know the requirements of the LORD.' The Hebrew word is mishpat, which is also the word for justice. In 5:4 and 5 the same expression is translated 'the justice of their God.' The two translations show the two sides of the word. It means the settled way God has ordered life, and it means the right that follows when that order is kept. The birds keep their appointed times without being told, but Israel will not keep God's.

The wound language is built on one root. In 8:11 the false prophets treat the shever of the people lightly, and in 8:21 Jeremiah says, 'For the brokenness of the daughter of my people I am crushed.' The word for 'brokenness' and the verb for 'I am crushed' share the root, shavar, to break. The prophet is broken by the break he sees. In the same verse he says he mourns, using a verb qadar which has the sense of going dark or wearing dark clothes, and speaks of horror. The grief shows on the body.

Knowing is the hidden theme of the second half. In 9:3 the liars 'do not take Me into account,' literally 'do not know Me.' In 9:6 they 'refuse to know Me.' Then in 9:24 the one who may boast is the one who 'understands and knows Me,' using the verb haskel, to act with insight, and yada, to know. The verb haskel is related to sakal, the word behind the 'foolish' of Jeremiah 5:21. The fools are those who lack the insight; the person who has it is the one who has come to know God.

The three things God delights in, in 9:24, are chesed, mishpat and tsedaqah, rendered by the BSB as 'loving devotion, justice and righteousness.' The BSB's footnote explains that chesed takes in love, kindness, faithfulness and loyalty to a covenant. The verb is stronger than it looks: God 'exercises' them, which means He does them. They are not ideals He admires but things He performs.

The word for lament in 9:20, qinah, is a technical term for the funeral song, which the prophets also use for their own songs of mourning over the nation. Jeremiah is asking the people to give a formal lament for themselves while they can still hear it.

Finally, the water of 8:14, 'poisoned water,' and 9:15 use the same Hebrew expression, and the plant of 9:15, 'wormwood,' is la'anah, a bitter herb. The word returns in Lamentations 3:15, 'He has intoxicated me with wormwood,' and the star Wormwood in Revelation 8:11 turns waters bitter. The bitterness of the covenant curses is carried into later writing.

typology.type: Jeremiah weeping over the city, Jeremiah 8:18 to 9:1
typology.fulfillment: Jesus 'saw the city, He wept over it,' Luke 19:41, and said, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace!' The correspondence is the grief of a messenger who loves the people he warns, and the same Jerusalem. The escalation is that Jeremiah could only wish to weep enough, while Jesus offers prayers 'with loud cries and tears,' Hebrews 5:7, and goes on to give His life for the city. At the tomb of Lazarus 'Jesus wept,' John 11:35. The type falls short in that Jeremiah's tears were a sign of judgment's coming, while Jesus' tears are joined to a rescue.

typology.type: The balm in Gilead and the physician, Jeremiah 8:22
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah's question has no answer in his day, but Jesus says, 'It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick,' Mark 2:17. He is not only a doctor but the one whose wounds heal: 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:5, quoted in 1 Peter 2:24. The correspondence is that a fatal wound meets its cure in a person. The text does not name the Messiah as the physician in Jeremiah 8, so the link is an echo of the picture, not a quotation. The type falls short because Gilead's balm was a physical remedy that was found wanting, while the healing in Christ is of the whole person and lasts.

typology.type: Boasting only in knowing the LORD, Jeremiah 9:23-24
typology.fulfillment: Paul quotes the call twice and ties it to Christ, 'who has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' 1 Corinthians 1:30-31. In Galatians 6:14 he becomes the example: 'may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.' The correspondence is exact because the God known in Jeremiah 9:24 is the God who has shown loving devotion, justice and righteousness at the cross. The pattern is limited because Jeremiah gave a command to the people, while Paul presents what Christ has given.

Judah has the sign but not the substance, and the New Testament names the substance: 'In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands,' Colossians 2:11. Paul says the true circumcision is 'of the heart, by the Spirit,' Romans 2:29, and that believers 'worship by the Spirit of God,' Philippians 3:3. The promise goes back to Deuteronomy 30:6, where the LORD says He will circumcise their hearts. The type falls short because the old sign was physical and external, and the fulfilment is an inward act done by God.

typology.type: The wailing women of Jerusalem, Jeremiah 9:17-20
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah summons women to lament over a city on its way to ruin. On the road to the cross a great crowd followed Jesus, 'including women who kept mourning and wailing for Him,' and He said, 'Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children,' Luke 23:27-28. The correspondence is of a lament over a city's coming judgment, spoken again at the foot of the cross. The text does not call these women a fulfilment of Jeremiah 9, so the link is an echo. The pattern falls short because the grief of Luke 23 is set beside an act that turns judgment aside.

study.christ:
The strongest connection is the shape of Jesus' ministry in Jerusalem. Jeremiah, forbidden to look away, weeps over a city that will not turn. Luke tells of Jesus, as He came near, seeing the city and weeping, 'If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes,' Luke 19:41-42. He picks up the lament of 8:20, the harvest passed and no salvation, and the unanswered question of 8:22, and answers it with Himself. He says elsewhere, 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... how often I have longed to gather your children together... but you were unwilling!' Matthew 23:37. The prophet's tears and the Lord's are not different tears but a single sorrow, and Hebrews says Jesus offered prayers and petitions 'with loud cries and tears,' Hebrews 5:7. The passage that leaves readers wondering whether God shares in the pain of His people is answered by One who 'wept' at a grave, John 11:35, and by One who 'took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows,' Isaiah 53:4.

The second connection is healing. The question 'Is there no balm in Gilead? Is no physician there?' is asked with no answer in sight, and the book goes on to say, 'Your injury is incurable,' Jeremiah 30:12, and then, 'I will bring to it health and healing,' Jeremiah 33:6. In the Gospels Jesus speaks of Himself as the doctor for the sick, Mark 2:17, and Peter says of the cross, 'By His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24. The One who heals does it by receiving the wound.

The third is knowing God. The unit ends with a call to boast in understanding and knowing the LORD, and Paul says that Christ is made 'wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption,' 1 Corinthians 1:30. Jesus says, 'this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent,' John 17:3. In Jeremiah 24:7 God promises, 'I will give them a heart to know Me,' and in 31:34, 'they will all know Me.' The knowledge the prophet says has failed is given by the one who makes the Father known, John 1:18.

The cry of 8:19, 'Is the LORD no longer in Zion? Is her King no longer there?', also has an ironic answer. Matthew says, 'See, your King comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey,' Matthew 21:5. The King whom the exiles feared had gone is the one who arrives, and the city that does not recognise Him is the city that Jeremiah lamented.

The heart circumcised in Christ completes the last verses. Colossians 2:11 says believers are circumcised by Christ, and Romans 2:29 says it is of the heart by the Spirit. What Judah lacked, and what the nations lacked, is given.

The reading needs care. Jeremiah's tears do not predict Jesus' tears in any coded way, and the Gospels do not say that Jesus was thinking of Jeremiah. What links them is that both love a rebellious city, and Christ brings to completion what the weeping prophet could only mourn.
study.god:
This is the passage in the book where God is most openly moved. 'Why have they provoked Me to anger with their carved images,' 8:19, is not the voice of a distant judge but of a God who takes betrayal personally. In 9:7 He asks, 'what else can I do because of the daughter of My people?', a question that sounds like exasperated love more than calm decision. Hosea has the same note, 'How could I give you up, O Ephraim?' Hosea 11:8. God is not unmoved by judgment; He suffers in His own sentence.

He is a God who knows what is said in secret. The picture of tongues like bows and friends who set traps, 9:3 to 8, comes from the God who hears the heart behind the greeting: 'With his mouth a man speaks peace to his neighbor, but in his heart he sets a trap for him.' The same God who watches the lies of the people sees the tears of the prophet. Nothing is hidden from Him in either direction.

He is a God who explains Himself. When the question comes, 'Why is the land destroyed?', 9:12, the LORD answers directly and does not leave His people to guess, 9:13 to 14. The reason is not that He was weak or absent but that they forsook His law. A God who gives reasons for His judgments is a God who intends people to understand and return. The earlier verses add that even creation was meant to teach, as the stork knows her seasons, 8:7.

He is a God who judges all nations. Verses 25 and 26 do not stop with Judah. Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert peoples are brought into the same sentence, because the issue is the heart and not the label. This guards the doctrine of God from becoming tribal. The LORD is not Judah's mascot but the Lord of the earth.

And He is a God defined by what He delights in. 'I am the LORD, who exercises loving devotion, justice and righteousness on the earth, for I delight in these things,' 9:24. This is one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament of what God is like. The three words form a character: faithful love, right order and right dealing. They are what He does, and they are what He wants known. The wise, the strong and the rich have their pride, but the only boast worth making is knowing a God like this. Micah 6:8 draws the same conclusion about what He requires.

There is a tension that the unit holds without resolving. The LORD announces destruction and weeps. He says He will 'refine them and test them' and yet declares He will make Jerusalem a heap of rubble. The Bible does not explain how these fit; it shows both, and the New Testament shows both coming together in the cross.

For worship, the unit invites believers to lament as well as to praise, and to bring to God a grief that matches His own. It also invites us to the only boast worth keeping.

crossReferences.note: Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and says it did not recognise the time of God's visit, then describes the city's destruction. The scene stands as the closest New Testament parallel to the prophet's tears, and shows the Lord sharing the sorrow Jeremiah could only voice.

Paul argues that God chose the foolish, weak and lowly so that no one may boast, and then quotes Jeremiah 9:23-24 as the conclusion: let him who boasts boast in the Lord. Christ is the wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption in which the boast is made.

Paul uses the same quotation to rebuke the Corinthians who boasted in their credentials. The text shows how an old prophetic principle still governed a first century argument about status, and how Paul expected believers to answer every claim to merit with the same line.

A man is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart by the Spirit. Paul takes the argument of Jeremiah 9:25-26 and says it directly: the sign without the substance counts for nothing.

Moses asks the people to circumcise their hearts and stiffen their necks no more. It shows that the charge of an uncircumcised heart was not Jeremiah's invention but a command at the foundation of the covenant.

Jesus says the sick, not the healthy, need a doctor. It answers Jeremiah's question about a physician and shows the Lord taking the role the prophet could not find, going to the broken and the sinful rather than waiting for those who think themselves well.
A caravan from Gilead carries balm to Egypt in Joseph's day. It shows why Jeremiah could ask about Gilead's balm, since it was the best known remedy in the world he knew.

The wound is called incurable and there is no remedy for the sores. Chapter 8 asks if there is a balm, and chapter 30 gives the grim answer, which then leads to the promise of healing in 30:17 and 33:6.

The ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's manger, but Israel does not know. It parallels Jeremiah 8:7, where the stork and the turtledove know their seasons. The prophets use animals to shame a people who ought to know better.

Paul has deep sorrow and unceasing anguish for his own people and could wish himself cut off for their sake. He shares the grief of Jeremiah 9:1, and shows how a servant of God is meant to feel toward those who refuse the message.
Streams of tears flow over the destruction of the daughter of my people. The book of Lamentations, traditionally linked to Jeremiah, takes the wish of 9:1 and turns it into fact after the fall.
What the LORD requires is to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God. It sets out in practical form the delight of Jeremiah 9:24, loving devotion, justice and righteousness.
Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent. The knowledge Jeremiah 9:24 declares to be the only boast is here defined as life itself and tied to the person of Christ.
God will wipe away every tear and there will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain. The weeping of Jeremiah 9:1 finds its answer in a world where the lament is over.

study.oneStory:
The grief of this unit has a source far back in the Bible. Before the flood, 'the LORD regretted that He had made man on the earth, and He was grieved in His heart,' Genesis 6:6. The first sin was an attempt to gain wisdom apart from God, since the tree was 'desirable for obtaining wisdom,' Genesis 3:6. Jeremiah 9:23 is the answer to that fall. The wise man is told not to boast in his wisdom, and the only knowledge worth having is to know the LORD. The Bible's story is partly a story of two kinds of knowing, and this unit sits at the point where the wrong kind has run its course and the right kind is named.

The wound of 8:21 and 22 has the same root. Sin is not a minor blemish but a fracture, and the old covenant had no balm for it. Circumcision, given to Abraham as a sign of the covenant, Genesis 17:10-11, was never meant to be the whole of the covenant. Jeremiah 9:25 and 26 says that a sign without a heart is empty, and so the story needs something more. Moses had already hinted at it, 'The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts,' Deuteronomy 30:6, and Jeremiah himself will say 'I will give them a heart to know Me,' Jeremiah 24:7, and 'they will all know Me,' Jeremiah 31:34. The new covenant is the answer to the uncircumcised heart.

The exile that this unit anticipates is the exile of Adam repeated. A people given a land and a law and warned of consequences lose the land and are scattered, 9:16. Yet the unit never leaves the thread of tears. God weeps, the prophet weeps, and the women are told to teach their daughters to lament, which means the story continues, since a people that can still lament has not given up on God.

The turning point is Christ. He weeps over the city, He is the physician, He is the wisdom and righteousness in which sinners can boast, and He carries out the circumcision of the heart. His death is the lament and the cure in one act. After Him the Spirit is given so that the heart really is changed, Ezekiel 36:26, and the people of God are drawn from every nation, with the nations that Jeremiah lists as uncircumcised now included among those who belong.

The story ends where the tears end. In the new creation, God 'will wipe away every tear from their eyes,' Revelation 21:4, and the leaves of the tree of life are 'for the healing of the nations,' Revelation 22:2. The balm of Gilead is finally found, and 'the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water,' Isaiah 11:9. What Jeremiah could only wish for is given to those who trust Him.

quiz.q: Why does Jeremiah say, is there no balm in Gilead?

options.text: Because Judah's wound from sin runs deeper than any earthly remedy can heal.
options.note: Verse 22 exposes that the nation's brokenness has gone past ordinary cure.

options.text: Because Gilead had literally run out of its famous medicinal resin.
options.note: The point is spiritual, not a literal shortage of trade goods.

options.text: Because Jeremiah had never actually visited Gilead.
options.note: The question is rhetorical, not about Jeremiah's travel history.

options.text: Because the coming exile would only be a temporary hardship.
options.note: The lament actually stresses that the wound is severe and unhealed, not minor.

quiz.q: What false comfort do the prophets and priests offer in 8:11?

options.text: They dress the wound of the people lightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there is no peace.
options.note: Verse 11 names this exact false reassurance.

options.text: They call the people to a public fast.
options.note: Fasting is not mentioned here; false comfort through empty words is the issue.

options.text: They warn the people honestly of coming judgment.
options.note: The opposite; their words are deceptively comforting, not honest warning.

options.text: They promise a swift military victory over Babylon.
options.note: The text speaks of false healing of a wound, a broader image than a specific military promise.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah wish for in 9:1?

options.text: That his head were a spring of water and his eyes a fountain of tears, to weep without ceasing over his people.
options.note: This wish gives Jeremiah his enduring title, the weeping prophet.

options.text: That he had never been called as a prophet at all.
options.note: That despair is not expressed here; his tears flow from love for his people, not regret over his calling.

options.text: That God would immediately destroy Judah's enemies.
options.note: Jeremiah's wish here is grief, not a call for vengeance.

options.text: That he could find a way to warn the people more persuasively.
options.note: Close to the spirit of the passage, but the specific wish in verse 1 is to weep, not to find better arguments.

quiz.q: According to 9:23-24, in what alone should a person boast?

options.text: In understanding and knowing the LORD, who delights in loving devotion, justice, and righteousness.
options.note: Verses 23 to 24 redirect all boasting away from wisdom, strength, and wealth to knowing God.

options.text: In wisdom gained through long study and learning.
options.note: Verse 23 explicitly excludes boasting in wisdom as the ultimate ground.

options.text: In personal strength and courage.
options.note: Verse 23 explicitly excludes boasting in strength.

options.text: In accumulated wealth and riches.
options.note: Verse 23 explicitly excludes boasting in riches.

quiz.q: What does God mean by calling Israel uncircumcised in heart in 9:25-26?

options.text: That they kept the outward covenant sign while their hearts remained untransformed and unfaithful.
options.note: The point is that the sign of the covenant was never meant to replace an inward, transformed loyalty to God.

options.text: That Israel had literally abandoned the practice of circumcision.
options.note: The charge concerns the heart, not a claim that the physical rite had been discontinued.

options.text: That circumcision was no longer required by God at all.
options.note: The passage does not abolish the sign; it exposes a heart that never matched the sign.

options.text: That only the surrounding nations needed any kind of circumcision.
options.note: The passage groups Israel with nations lacking the sign altogether, but the deeper charge is specifically about Israel's uncircumcised heart.

questions: Jeremiah wished his eyes were a fountain of tears over his people's sin. What griefs in your own life or community do you tend to numb rather than feel honestly before God?
The false prophets cried Peace, peace, when there was no peace. Where might you be settling for comfortable words instead of the harder truth you actually need to hear?
God says the only right boast is knowing Him, not wisdom, strength, or wealth. What do you find yourself most tempted to boast in instead?
Judah carried the sign of the covenant while their hearts remained far from God. Where might your outward religious practice be running ahead of an actual transformed heart?
Jesus wept over Jerusalem exactly as Jeremiah wept centuries before. How does knowing that Christ still grieves over hardened hearts change how you pray for those who resist Him?

translationNotes.note: The phrase balm in Gilead became so memorable that it later entered English idiom and hymnody; tsori refers to a specific medicinal resin for which the region of Gilead was known in trade.

In the Hebrew Bible's chapter division, this verse is actually the final verse of chapter 8, numbered 8:23; English translations including the BSB follow the chapter break adopted in most modern Bibles, so the verse numbers in chapter 9 run one behind the Hebrew text throughout much of the chapter.

The three Hebrew words rendered loving devotion, justice, and righteousness, hesed, mishpat, and tsedaqah, form a compact summary of God's own character that recurs throughout the Prophets and Psalms.
